section_1.title: Scalars vs. Vectors: The Treasure Map
section_1.content: Introduce the fundamental difference between a scalar (magnitude only) and a vector (magnitude and direction). Explain that while a scalar tells us 'how much,' a vector tells us 'where to go.'
section_1.example: An explorer cat is told there is treasure 5 miles away (Scalar). Without direction, the cat wanders in circles. But if the map says '5 miles East' (Vector), the cat finds the treasure immediately.

section_2.title: Prerequisite: The Coordinate Grid
section_2.content: Briefly review the Cartesian coordinate system (x and y axes) as the 'playground' for vectors. Explain how points are located using (x, y) coordinates.
section_2.example: A bird is perched on a grid at point (0,0). To reach a worm at (3, 2), the bird needs to understand its relative position on the x (horizontal) and y (vertical) axes.

section_3.title: Visualizing Vectors as Arrows
section_3.content: Define a vector mathematically as an arrow starting from the origin (0,0) to a point (x, y). Introduce notation like v = [x, y]. Emphasize that the length of the arrow represents 'Magnitude' and the tip points in the 'Direction'.
section_3.example: A drone flies from the starting pad (0,0) to a delivery point at (4, 3). We represent this flight as a bold arrow. Visually, the drone moved 4 units right and 3 units up.

section_4.title: Vector Addition: The 'Head-to-Tail' Rule
section_4.content: Explain how to combine two movements. When you add vector A to vector B, you place the 'tail' of B at the 'head' of A. The resulting vector (the sum) is the shortcut from the start of A to the end of B.
section_4.example: An ant walks 3 units East (Vector A), then turns and walks 2 units North (Vector B). The total displacement is the diagonal vector C, which connects the ant's starting point directly to its final destination.

section_5.title: Scalar Multiplication: Scaling the Force
section_5.content: Show what happens when a vector is multiplied by a single number (a scalar). Multiplying by a number > 1 stretches it; between 0 and 1 shrinks it; a negative number reverses its direction.
section_5.example: A robot character has a 'Jump Vector' of [1, 2]. When it picks up a 'Power Boost' (scalar = 2), its jump becomes [2, 4], doubling the height and distance of the leap.

section_6.title: Summary and Real-World Application
section_6.content: Consolidate the points: Vectors combine direction and size. Mention that this math is the foundation of modern video game physics and satellite navigation.
section_6.example: In a racing game, the car's velocity is a vector. Every frame, the computer adds the 'Acceleration Vector' to the 'Velocity Vector' to determine exactly where the car should move on the screen.

        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

section_1.content: Introduce the fundamental difference between a scalar (magnitude only) and a vector (magnitude and direction). Explain that while a scalar tells us 'how much,' a vector tells us 'where to go.'
section_1.example: An explorer cat is told there is treasure 5 miles away (Scalar). Without direction, the cat wanders in circles. But if the map says '5 miles East' (Vector), the cat finds the treasure immediately.

section_2.title: Prerequisite: The Coordinate Grid
section_2.content: Briefly review the Cartesian coordinate system (x and y axes) as the 'playground' for vectors. Explain how points are located using (x, y) coordinates.
section_2.example: A bird is perched on a grid at point (0,0). To reach a worm at (3, 2), the bird needs to understand its relative position on the x (horizontal) and y (vertical) axes.

section_3.title: Visualizing Vectors as Arrows
section_3.content: Define a vector mathematically as an arrow starting from the origin (0,0) to a point (x, y). Introduce notation like v = [x, y]. Emphasize that the length of the arrow represents 'Magnitude' and the tip points in the 'Direction'.
section_3.example: A drone flies from the starting pad (0,0) to a delivery point at (4, 3). We represent this flight as a bold arrow. Visually, the drone moved 4 units right and 3 units up.

section_4.title: Vector Addition: The 'Head-to-Tail' Rule
section_4.content: Explain how to combine two movements. When you add vector A to vector B, you place the 'tail' of B at the 'head' of A. The resulting vector (the sum) is the shortcut from the start of A to the end of B.
section_4.example: An ant walks 3 units East (Vector A), then turns and walks 2 units North (Vector B). The total displacement is the diagonal vector C, which connects the ant's starting point directly to its final destination.

section_5.title: Scalar Multiplication: Scaling the Force
section_5.content: Show what happens when a vector is multiplied by a single number (a scalar). Multiplying by a number > 1 stretches it; between 0 and 1 shrinks it; a negative number reverses its direction.
section_5.example: A robot character has a 'Jump Vector' of [1, 2]. When it picks up a 'Power Boost' (scalar = 2), its jump becomes [2, 4], doubling the height and distance of the leap.

section_6.title: Summary and Real-World Application
section_6.content: Consolidate the points: Vectors combine direction and size. Mention that this math is the foundation of modern video game physics and satellite navigation.
section_6.example: In a racing game, the car's velocity is a vector. Every frame, the computer adds the 'Acceleration Vector' to the 'Velocity Vector' to determine exactly where the car should move on the screen.

section_1.title: Scalars vs. Vectors: The Treasure Map
lecture_lines: Scalars represent a magnitude or quantity, like distance.
Vectors combine magnitude with a specific direction.
A scalar tells us how much; vectors show where.
animations: Text: Scalars only have magnitude or size. Anim: A number '5' appears in white #FFFFFF, then a circle with radius 5 slowly pulses.
Text: Vectors have both magnitude and direction. Anim: An arrow (vector) appears in yellow #FFFF00, pointing to the right, labeled '5 miles East'.
Text: Without direction, we wander in circles. Anim: A small dot (explorer cat) [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/cat.png] moves in a chaotic circle around the origin.

Text: Direction leads us straight to the goal. Anim: The dot [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/cat.png] moves in a straight line along the yellow arrow to a treasure icon [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/treasure.svg] at the end.
Text: Vectors tell us exactly where to go. Anim: The yellow arrow flashes twice, and the text 'Vector' highlights in yellow #FFFF00.

section_2.title: Prerequisite: The Coordinate Grid
lecture_lines: The coordinate grid is our mathematical playground.
We locate points using horizontal and vertical coordinates.
Every position is defined by an (x, y) pair.
animations: Text: The grid is our mathematical playground. Anim: A coordinate grid with white #FFFFFF axes and grey #808080 lines fades in.
Text: Points are defined by (x, y) coordinates. Anim: A point appears at (3, 2) in cyan #00FFFF, labeled with text '(3, 2)'.
Text: We measure horizontal and vertical distances. Anim: A dashed line moves from (0,0) to (3,0), then up to (3,2) in cyan #00FFFF.

section_3.title: Visualizing Vectors as Arrows
lecture_lines: We represent vectors as arrows starting from the origin.
The arrow's length shows the vector's magnitude.
The tip points in the vector's specific direction.
animations: Text: A vector starts at the origin (0,0). Anim: A bold blue #0000FF arrow grows from (0,0) to (4, 3).
Text: The tip points in the vector's direction. Anim: The arrowhead of the blue arrow flashes in light blue #ADD8E6.
Text: The length represents the vector's magnitude. Anim: A bracket appears next to the arrow labeled 'Magnitude' in blue #0000FF.
Text: We write this vector as v = [4, 3]. Anim: The mathematical notation 'v = [4, 3]' appears in blue #0000FF at the top.
Text: This means 4 right and 3 up. Anim: The horizontal and vertical components of the arrow are highlighted in green #00FF00.

section_4.title: Vector Addition: The 'Head-to-Tail' Rule
lecture_lines: To add vectors, place one tail at another's head.
The sum is the shortcut from start to finish.
This "head-to-tail" rule combines two different movements.
animations: Text: Place the tail of B at A's head. Anim: Vector A (red #FF0000) is shown, then Vector B (green #00FF00) moves so its tail is at A's tip.
Text: The sum is the shortcut path. Anim: A new vector C (magenta #FF00FF) is drawn from the start of A to the end of B.
Text: This represents the total displacement. Anim: The magenta arrow C pulses while A and B fade slightly.
Text: Walking East then North equals the diagonal. Anim: [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/dot.svg] follows the path of A, then B, then moves directly along C.
Text: We write this as A + B = C. Anim: The equation 'A + B = C' appears in white #FFFFFF, with colors matching the arrows.

section_5.title: Scalar Multiplication: Scaling the Force
lecture_lines: Multiplying a vector by a scalar changes its length.
Positive scalars stretch or shrink the arrow's size.
Negative scalars flip the vector's direction completely.
animations: Text: Scalars can stretch or shrink a vector. Anim: An orange #FFA500 vector [1, 2] appears, then stretches to [2, 4].
Text: Multiplying by 2 doubles the vector's length. Anim: The label '2 * v' appears, and the vector flashes in orange #FFA500.
Text: Negative scalars reverse the vector's direction. Anim: The vector rotates 180 degrees and points the opposite way, changing to red #FF0000.

Master vectors to understand how the world moves.

from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section4Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        title_text = "Vector Addition: The 'Head-to-Tail' Rule"
        lecture_lines = [
            "To add vectors, place one tail at another's head.",
            "The sum is the shortcut from start to finish.",
            "This 'head-to-tail' rule combines two different movements."
        ]
        self.setup_layout(title_text, lecture_lines)

        # Define Colors
        color_a = "#FF0000" # Red
        color_b = "#00FF00" # Green
        color_c = "#FF00FF" # Magenta

        # Define Mobjects for Stage 1: Vector A and B
        # Vector A: starts at C2, ends at C5 (Length 3 East)
        v_a = Arrow(start=self.grid["C2"], end=self.grid["C5"], color=color_a, buff=0)
        label_a = MathTex(r"\vec{A}", color=color_a)
        self.place_at_grid(label_a, "D3", scale_factor=0.8)

        # B initially separate (Length 2 North)
        v_b_start_init = self.grid["F2"]
        v_b_end_init = self.grid["D2"]
        v_b = Arrow(start=v_b_start_init, end=v_b_end_init, color=color_b, buff=0)
        label_b = MathTex(r"\vec{B}", color=color_b)
        self.place_at_grid(label_b, "E3", scale_factor=0.8)

        # Define target for B (Head of A to A5)
        target_v_b_start = self.grid["C5"]
        v_b_shift = target_v_b_start - v_b_start_init

        # Define Stage 2: Vector C (Resultant)
        v_c = Arrow(start=self.grid["C2"], end=self.grid["A5"], color=color_c, buff=0)
        label_c = MathTex(r"\vec{C}", color=color_c)
        self.place_at_grid(label_c, "B3", scale_factor=0.8)

        # Define Stage 5: Equation
        eq_a = MathTex(r"\vec{A}", color=color_a)
        plus = MathTex("+", color=WHITE)
        eq_b = MathTex(r"\vec{B}", color=color_b)
        equals = MathTex("=", color=WHITE)
        eq_c = MathTex(r"\vec{C}", color=color_c)
        equation = VGroup(eq_a, plus, eq_b, equals, eq_c).arrange(RIGHT, buff=0.2)
        self.place_in_area(equation, "F2", "F5", scale_factor=1.0)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # "To add vectors, place one tail at another's head."
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(YELLOW))
        self.play(Create(v_a), Write(label_a))
        self.wait(0.5)
        self.play(Create(v_b), Write(label_b))
        self.wait(1)
        # Place tail of B at head of A
        self.play(
            v_b.animate.shift(v_b_shift),
            label_b.animate.shift(v_b_shift),
            run_time=2
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # "The sum is the shortcut from start to finish."
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(color_c))
        self.play(Create(v_c), Write(label_c))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # "This 'head-to-tail' rule combines two different movements."
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(WHITE))
        
        # Pulse Vector C while A and B fade slightly
        self.play(
            v_a.animate.set_stroke(opacity=0.3),
            label_a.animate.set_fill(opacity=0.3),
            v_b.animate.set_stroke(opacity=0.3),
            label_b.animate.set_fill(opacity=0.3),
            run_time=1
        )
        # Pulse animation
        self.play(v_c.animate.set_stroke(width=10), run_time=0.5)
        self.play(v_c.animate.set_stroke(width=4), run_time=0.5)
        self.wait(0.5)
        
        # Dot following the path (Walking East then North)
        dot = Dot(color=WHITE, radius=0.1)
        dot.move_to(self.grid["C2"])
        self.play(FadeIn(dot))
        # Move East along A
        self.play(dot.animate.move_to(self.grid["C5"]), run_time=1, rate_func=linear)
        # Move North along B
        self.play(dot.animate.move_to(self.grid["A5"]), run_time=1, rate_func=linear)
        self.wait(0.5)
        # Move along diagonal C
        self.play(dot.animate.move_to(self.grid["C2"]), run_time=0.1) # teleport back to start
        self.play(dot.animate.move_to(self.grid["A5"]), run_time=1.5, rate_func=linear)
        self.play(FadeOut(dot))

        # Show the vector addition equation
        self.play(Write(equation))
        self.wait(2)
